chapter.name: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
chapter.blurb: The Cartesian plane, quadrants, distances between points, reflections in the axes and the midpoint of a segment.

scope_in.item: Name the axes, origin and quadrants of the Cartesian plane and use a scale to place points
Write and read the coordinates of a point and tell its quadrant from the signs
Coordinates of points on the axes; distance between points on a line parallel to an axis; (x, y) versus (y, x)
Find the distance between any two points using the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem
Find the reflection of a point or a triangle in the x-axis or y-axis and see that lengths are preserved
Find and use the midpoint of a segment, trisection points, points on or inside a circle, using coordinates (starred end-of-chapter exercises)

scope_out.item: Equation of a line, slope and gradient
scope_out.reason: Not in this chapter; later coordinate geometry

scope_out.item: Section formula in general ratio m : n
scope_out.reason: Only the midpoint and trisection ideas appear, discovered in exercises
The chapter deals only with the 2-D plane

scope_out.reason: Only reflection in the axes is used

concepts.name: The coordinate plane, axes and origin
concepts.description: Two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, meeting at the origin, used to locate points in 2-D space.
concepts.idea: One number locates a point on a line; a flat surface needs two numbers, so we use two perpendicular number lines.
concepts.rule: The horizontal line is the x-axis, the vertical line is the y-axis and they meet at the origin O (0, 0). Right and up are positive; left and down are negative.
concepts.example: On a floor map with scale 1 cm : 1 foot, a corner of the room is placed at the origin and the two walls lie along the axes.

concepts.example: S (3, -5) has x = 3 and y = -5, so it lies in Quadrant IV; Q (-5, 3) lies in Quadrant II.

questions.q: Meera says: "Every point with a positive x-coordinate is in Quadrant I." Is she right?

concepts.name: Points on the axes and distances parallel to the axes
concepts.description: Coordinates of points on the axes, the difference between (x, y) and (y, x), and distances along a line parallel to an axis.
concepts.idea: A point on the x-axis has y = 0 and a point on the y-axis has x = 0; two points with the same y-coordinate are a horizontal distance apart.
concepts.rule: Points on the x-axis are (x, 0); on the y-axis (0, y). The distance between (x1, y) and (x2, y) is |x2 - x1|; between (x, y1) and (x, y2) it is |y2 - y1|. (x, y) = (y, x) only when x = y.
concepts.example: B (4.5, 0) is 4.5 units right of O on the x-axis; G (0, -4.5) is 4.5 units below O on the y-axis.

concepts.name: Distance between two points
concepts.description: Finding the distance between any two points of the plane with the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.
concepts.idea: Moving from one point to another is a shift along the x-axis and a shift along the y-axis, which are the two legs of a right triangle.
concepts.rule: Distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2). It does not matter whether the differences are positive or negative.
concepts.example: A (3, 4) and D (7, 1): shifts 4 and 3, so AD = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 units.

concepts.name: Reflection of points in the axes
concepts.description: Coordinates of the mirror image of a point in the x-axis or y-axis, and what a reflection preserves.
concepts.idea: A mirror image is at the same distance from the mirror axis on the opposite side.
concepts.rule: Reflection in the y-axis: (x, y) goes to (-x, y). Reflection in the x-axis: (x, y) goes to (x, -y). Lengths are preserved.
concepts.example: A (3, 4) reflected in the y-axis gives A' (-3, 4); triangle ADM keeps side lengths 5, sqrt(29), sqrt(40).

concepts.name: Midpoints and solving problems with coordinates
concepts.description: Discovering the midpoint rule and using coordinates and distances to solve problems on segments, circles and triangles (end-of-chapter exercises).
concepts.idea: The midpoint of a segment is halfway between its ends in both directions, so each coordinate of M is the average of the ends' coordinates.
concepts.rule: If M is the midpoint of S (x1, y1) and T (x2, y2) then M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). A point is within, on or outside a circle centred at O by comparing its distance from O with the radius.
concepts.example: M (-7, 1) is the midpoint of A (3, -4) and B (x, y): (3 + x)/2 = -7 gives x = -17 and (-4 + y)/2 = 1 gives y = 6.
